name: Apache Subversion
summary: The centralized version control system that replaced CVS: one server holds the history as a single numbered sequence of atomic commits, and clients check out any directory of it.
intro: A Subversion (SVN) repository lives on one server and records the whole tree of files and directories over time. Every commit is atomic, all of its changes go in or none do, and gets the next repository-wide revision number, so `r1234` names the state of the entire tree after that commit, not of one file. Clients check out a working copy of any directory, with a hidden `.svn` directory that keeps each file’s original contents, so `svn status` and `svn diff` against your own edits work offline. Anything involving history (commit, log, blame, diffs between revisions) goes to the server. The default FSFS back end stores each revision’s changes in a single file on disk.

Branches and tags are just copies. `svn copy` of `trunk` to `branches/fix-login` takes constant time because the server stores a pointer to the existing tree, like a hard link; `trunk`, `branches` and `tags` are a convention, not something Subversion knows about. Because everything is a path, access control is too: path-based authorization can let one group write to a single directory and others only read it. For files that can’t be merged, such as images, `svn lock` gives one person the right to commit a file, and the `svn:needs-lock` property keeps it read-only on disk until you take the lock.

CollabNet started Subversion in 2000 as a better CVS, and it has been an Apache Software Foundation top-level project since February 2010. Git has long since overtaken it: 5% of Stack Overflow’s 2022 survey respondents used Subversion, against 94% for Git. The latest release is 1.15.0 (October 8, 2026), the first new release line since 1.14 in 2020. It can leave the original file copies out of a working copy and fetch them on demand, which its notes say cuts working-copy storage by up to 50%, and every release line is now supported for at least three years.
strengths: A simple model: one server, one sequence of revision numbers, and no local history to keep in sync
Check out just the directory you need, at whatever depth, and grant read or write access per directory
Locking and `svn:needs-lock` stop two people editing the same unmergeable binary file
Mature and conservative: 1.15 still works with 1.8 working copies and reads older repositories without a dump and reload
limits: No local commits: committing, browsing history and blame all need a connection to the server
Subversion has no concept of a branch, only copies of directories, so branch structure is up to your team’s conventions
A shrinking ecosystem: GitHub removed its Subversion support in January 2024, and most tools assume Git
Working copies in the new 1.15 format, needed for pristines on demand, can’t be read by 1.14 or older clients

snippet.title: Create a repository, branch by copying, lock a binary file
source: svnadmin create /var/svn/shop                 # a new FSFS repository
-m "Branch for the login fix"              # a cheap server-side copy
svn propset svn:needs-lock yes art/hero.psd   # read-only until locked
svn commit -m "New hero art"                  # one atomic revision; releases the lock
svn checkout $REPO/trunk/docs --depth immediates   # just one directory, one level deep

story: By 2000 CVS was the standard open-source version control system, and CollabNet used it in its collaboration software. It wanted something better. In February 2000 it approached Karl Fogel, the author of a book on CVS, who was already discussing a new design with Jim Blandy; Blandy had coined the name Subversion and sketched the data store. CollabNet hired Fogel, and the team set out not to break new ground but to fix CVS: keep its model and features, drop its bugs and misfeatures, and make switching easy. After 14 months of coding, Subversion became self-hosting on August 31, 2001.

Version 1.0 shipped on February 23, 2004. Version 1.2 in May 2005 added optional file locking and made FSFS, which keeps revisions as plain files instead of in a Berkeley DB database, the default. Version 1.5 in June 2008 added merge tracking, and 1.7 in October 2011 replaced the scattered per-directory metadata with a single `.svn` directory at the root of each working copy. CollabNet brought the project to the Apache Incubator in November 2009, and in February 2010 it became a top-level project and Apache Subversion.

Git and GitHub overtook it, and GitHub turned off its Subversion support in January 2024. But at its 20th anniversary in 2020, Fogel said Subversion was still widely used, especially in enterprise settings, for its reliability, its handling of large files and its path-based authorization. Development continued: 1.15.0 arrived on October 8, 2026, more than six years after 1.14.

choices.choice: Fix CVS rather than reinvent version control
choices.why: CVS tracked only individual files, so it couldn’t version directories or record renames and copies, and a commit could land half-way. Subversion kept the CVS working style, check out, edit, update, commit, but versioned whole directory trees and made every commit atomic.

choices.choice: One revision number for the whole repository
choices.why: Unlike most version control systems, whose revision numbers applied to individual files, each Subversion commit creates a new numbered state of the entire tree, so one number identifies exactly what the project looked like after any commit.

choices.choice: Branches and tags as cheap copies
choices.why: Rather than a separate branching mechanism, Subversion makes a copy that stores only a pointer to the existing tree, in constant time. Branches and tags are then just directories, with history the same tools can show.

choices.choice: Add optional locking for files that can’t be merged
choices.why: Merging works for text but not for images or other binaries, where two people’s edits can’t be combined. Version 1.2 added `svn lock` and `svn:needs-lock` so teams could serialize work on such files while still merging everything else.
